## Faust: Advanced Synthesis (1/2) {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 88%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
:::
  - *Waveform or Wavetable synthesis* is not the only method that we can use in order to create sound. We can also use ***additive synthesis***, which is a superposition of oscillators running at different frequencies. One really fast way to do this in Faust is to use the ***par*** operator, which puts signal expressions ***in parallel*** dynamically.
:::
:::

<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
## Faust: Advanced Synthesis (1/2) {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
  - **Frequency-modulation** (***FM***) **synthesis** is another well-known
   synthesis method, which implies *inter-modulated oscillator graphs*.
:::
  - In **FM**, the modulator makes the carrier's **frequency** go up and down, very fast (at audio rate).
  - The **index** sets *how far* the frequency moves: the higher the index, the **brighter** the sound.
  - This creates new frequencies around the carrier, called **sidebands**, evenly spaced by the modulator's frequency.
  - When the modulator and carrier frequencies are in a **simple ratio** (×1, ×2, ×3...), the sidebands fall on harmonics: **harmonic** sound. Otherwise: **inharmonic** (bells, metallic sounds).
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.content style="padding-left: 5%; width: 110%;"}
{{< fm preset=simple >}}
:::
:::
::::

<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
## Faust: Advanced Synthesis (1/2) {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
  - **Frequency-modulation** (***FM***) **synthesis** is another well-known
   synthesis method, which implies *inter-modulated oscillator graphs*.
:::
  - Each oscillator is called an **operator**: it can be a **carrier** (heard) or a **modulator** (modulates another operator).
  - Operators can be combined in **graphs** (called *algorithms* on the Yamaha **DX7**):
    - **stacks** (a modulator modulating a modulator), 
    - **parallel** modulators, 
    - one modulator shared by **several carriers**, 
    - **feedback** (an operator modulating itself, with `~` in Faust!).
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.content style="padding-left: 5%; width: 110%;"}
{{< fm preset=stack >}}
:::
:::
::::

<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
## Faust: Advanced Synthesis (1/2) {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
  - **Frequency-modulation** (***FM***) **synthesis** is another well-known
   synthesis method, which implies *inter-modulated oscillator graphs*.
:::
  - **Ring modulation** (*multiplying* two signals, see *Faust: Basics*) also creates sidebands, but only **two**: at the **sum** and at the **difference** of the two frequencies. The carrier itself **disappears**.
  - In **AM**, the modulator has an *offset*: the carrier **stays**, with its two sidebands.
  - With a *rich* carrier, **every harmonic** gets its own pair of sidebands: the result is usually **inharmonic**.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.content style="padding-left: 5%; width: 110%;"}
{{< ringmod >}}
:::
:::
::::

## Faust: Advanced Synthesis (2/2) {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 95%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
:::
  - ***Physical model synthesis*** consists in ***emulating the physical properties
  of an instrument*** in order to reproduce its sound. 
  Different methods exist in order to achieve this: 
  **modal synthesis**, **FDTD**, **digital waveguides**, *etc.* 
:::
:::

## Faust: Advanced Synthesis (2/2) {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 95%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
  - ***Physical model synthesis*** consists in ***emulating the physical properties of an instrument*** in order to reproduce its sound. Different methods exist in order to achieve this: **modal synthesis**, **FDTD**, **digital waveguides**, *etc.* 
  - Faust has in its ***libraries*** ('pm' prefix) a good collection  of ***physically-modeled instruments*** (*flutes*, *bells*, *guitars*, *voice*, *etc.*). 
:::
  - ***Granular synthesis*** is a method which uses overlapping '***grains***' (short fragments of sound, around **1 to 100 milliseconds**) from a ***buffer***, which are going to be played at *different speeds*, *phases*, *volume* and *frequency*.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
```{.js code-line-numbers="|" filename="faust/examples/synthesis/granular.dsp"}
{{< include /faust/examples/synthesis/granular.dsp >}}
```
{{< faust faust/examples/synthesis/granular.dsp >}}
:::
